# Membership data formats {#sec-formats}

The diagram below illustrates a minimal cross-referencing example consisting of two classifications with two concepts each, linked by fuzzy membership values [@Zadeh_1965; @IUCN_2025].

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
    CLASS1:::Clas
    CLASS2:::Clas
    subgraph CLASS1 ["Source classification"]
        ECO1(["Concept A"]):::Ecos
        ECO2(["Concept B"]):::Ecos
    end
    subgraph CLASS2 ["Target classification"]
        ECO3(["Concept Z"]):::Ecos
        ECO4(["Concept W"]):::Ecos
    end

    ECO1 ==>|100%| ECO3
    ECO1 -.->|0%| ECO4
    ECO2 -->|60%| ECO3
    ECO2 -->|40%| ECO4

    classDef Ecos fill:#dfd,stroke:#040,color:#040, stroke-width:2px
    classDef Clas fill:#fff,stroke:#040,color:#040, stroke-width:2px
```

These relationships can be represented in three main tabular formats, each suited to a different stage of data entry or computation.

## Membership matrix

A membership matrix places source concepts in rows and target concepts in columns:

| | Concept Z | Concept W |
|---|---|---|
| Concept A | 100% | 0% |
| Concept B | 40% | 60% |

The dimensions grow with the product of both classifications ($n$ rows for the source and $m$ columns for the target). Matrices expose zero and non-zero memberships transparently and are convenient for spreadsheet entry (used by `AK_V1` and `AL_V2` in @sec-input-memb) and numerical distance calculations—in `ecoSynthesis`, `membership_matrix()` builds a 3D `[source, target, interpreter]` array directly from a long-format `membership_tbl` for `calc_agreement()`. However, 2D matrices become unwieldy for storing multi-round metadata and sparse large classifications.

## Long-format table

A long-format membership table stores one `(source, target, membership)` link per row:

| Source Classification | Target Classification | Membership |
|---|---|---|
| Concept A | Concept Z | 100% |
| Concept B | Concept W | 60% |
| Concept B | Concept Z | 40% |

The table has only three core columns (plus interpreter/round metadata) and shrinks substantially when zero-membership rows are omitted. This is the canonical analytical format used by `ecoSynthesis::membership_tbl()` and all downstream validation, entropy, plotting, and synthesis functions in this workflow.

## Paired-column (wide) format

A paired-column table stores up to $q$ target–membership pairs per source row:

| Source Concept | Target Concept 1 | Membership | Target Concept 2 | Membership |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Concept A | Concept Z | 100% | | |
| Concept B | Concept W | 60% | Concept Z | 40% |

This format has $n$ rows and a fixed number of columns ($1 + 2q$). It is compact for manual expert elicitation (used by seven of the nine CSV files in `xrefdata/`) and can be standardised with `ecoSynthesis::standardise_xref_pairs()` and reshaped to long format via `ecoSynthesis::import_paired_membership()` or `scripts/functions.R::pivot_wide_membership_table()` (see @sec-input-memb).

## Incorporating multiple interpreters and rounds

Long-format tables scale naturally to multiple interpreters, elicitation rounds, dates, and methods by adding metadata columns:

| Source | Target | Membership | Interpreter | Date | Methods |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Concept A | Concept Z | 100% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2011 | Match descriptions |
| Concept B | Concept W | 60% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2011 | Match descriptions |
| Concept B | Concept Z | 40% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2011 | Match descriptions |
| Concept A | Concept Z | 80% | Interpreter B | 25 May 2025 | Compare attributes |
| Concept A | Concept W | 20% | Interpreter B | 25 May 2025 | Compare attributes |
| Concept B | Concept W | 80% | Interpreter B | 25 May 2025 | Compare attributes |
| Concept B | Concept Z | 20% | Interpreter B | 25 May 2025 | Compare attributes |
| Concept A | Concept Z | 100% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2026 | Revised opinion |
| Concept B | Concept W | 60% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2026 | Revised opinion |
| Concept B | Concept Z | 40% | Interpreter A | 25 May 2026 | Revised opinion |
